title: Comparing two sequences
objectives: Recover the subsequence by walking back through the table
Adapt the same table to edit distance

screens.title: Letters in order
screens.prose: A **subsequence** keeps letters in their order but may skip some: ACE is a subsequence of ABCDE. We want the longest subsequence that HEDGE and EDGY share.
screens.question: Tap the letters of HEDGE that make the longest common subsequence.

hints.text: Read EDGY from the left. Which of its letters appear in HEDGE, in the same order?
EDGY has no H, and its only E comes before D.
E, D and G appear in this order in both words. Y is not in HEDGE.

feedback.correct: E, D, G: three letters, in order, in both words.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each tapped letter must appear in EDGY too, in the same order.

byKey.edge: EDGE needs two Es in EDGY, and EDGY has one. Drop the last E.
byKey.r1c1: H is not in EDGY at all.
byKey.r1c5: This E comes after G in HEDGE, but EDGY's only E comes before G.

explain.text: EDG is common to both, and no four-letter subsequence is: EDGY has one E and HEDGE has no Y. Checking every subsequence of a 20-letter word means over a million of them. For two 20-letter words, a table needs about 400 cells.

screens.title: Prefixes
screens.prose: Shrink the problem to **prefixes**: the first $i$ letters of HEDGE against the first $j$ of EDGY. Row ∅ and column ∅ are empty prefixes, so they hold 0. Row H is all 0: EDGY has no H.
screens.question: How long is the longest common subsequence of HE and E?

hints.text: Which letters do HE and E share?
This is the cell for row E, column E.
HE and E share the letter E, so the length is 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the letters of HE that are also in E.

byKey.zero: HE ends in E, and E is the whole of the other prefix. They share it.
byKey.two: E is a single letter, so a common subsequence has at most one letter.

explain.text: Call this cell $\text{lcs}[2][1]$: the longest common subsequence of the first 2 letters of $a$ and the first 1 of $b$. Every cell is one such pair of prefixes. The corner, $\text{lcs}[5][4]$, is the whole problem.

screens.title: When the letters match
screens.prose: Rows ∅ to E are filled. Now $\text{lcs}[3][2]$: HED against ED. Both prefixes end in D, so that D can pair with D and close the subsequence.
screens.question: Tap the one cell that $\text{lcs}[3][2]$ adds 1 to.

hints.text: Pair the two final Ds. What is left of each prefix?
Remove D from both: HE and E.
HE against E is $\text{lcs}[2][1]$, one row up and one column left.

feedback.correct: The diagonal: HE against E, which is 1. So $\text{lcs}[3][2] = 2$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Remove the matched D from both prefixes and find that cell.

byKey.r3c3: That is HE against ED. It still holds $b$'s D, which is already paired with $a$'s D.
byKey.r4c2: That is HED against E. It still holds $a$'s D, which is already paired.
byKey.r4c3: That is the cell being filled. Tap the cell it builds on.

explain.text: A matched pair uses the last letter of both prefixes. What is left is HE against E, the diagonal cell, so $\text{lcs}[3][2] = 1 + 1 = 2$. The pair ED is the subsequence so far.

screens.title: When they differ
screens.prose: When the last letters differ, one of them is unpaired. Drop $a$'s letter (the cell above) or $b$'s letter (the cell to the left), and keep the larger.
screens.question: Fill row D: $\text{lcs}[3][j]$ for $j = 1$ to $4$.

hints.text: Only column D is a match. The others take the larger of up and left.
D against E: up is 1, left is 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add 1 to the diagonal only on a match; otherwise take the larger of up and left.

byKey.r0c1: D and E differ. Up (HE against E) is 1 and left is 0: keep 1.
byKey.r0c2: D matches D: the diagonal is 1, so this cell is 2.
byKey.r0c3: D and G differ. Up is 1 and left is 2: keep 2. Do not add 1 without a match.
byKey.r0c4: D and Y differ. Up is 1 and left is 2: keep 2.

explain.text: Only the D column matched. Every other cell copied the larger neighbour, so the row never drops below its left or upper cell.

screens.title: Finish the table
screens.prose: Two rows left. The rule is the same: match, diagonal plus 1; no match, the larger of up and left.
screens.question: Fill rows G and E.

hints.text: Find the matches first: G against G, and E against E.
G against G: the diagonal is $\text{lcs}[3][2] = 2$.
Row G: 1, 2, 3, 3. Row E: E matches E with diagonal 0, so 1; then 2, 3, 3 from the larger neighbour.

feedback.correct: Both rows end in 3: the corner is 3, the EDG you found.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each cell for a match first.

byKey.r0c3: G matches G: the diagonal $\text{lcs}[3][2]$ is 2, so 3.
byKey.r1c1: E matches E. The diagonal is $\text{lcs}[4][0] = 0$, so this cell is 1.
byKey.r1c3: E and G differ. Up is 3: keep it.
byKey.r1c4: E and Y differ. Up and left are both 3.

explain.text: The corner $\text{lcs}[5][4] = 3$, the length of EDG. The final E of HEDGE added nothing: EDGY's E was used up early.

screens.title: Read the letters back
screens.prose: Walk back from the corner. On a match, step diagonally and keep that letter. Otherwise step to the larger of up and left, going up on a tie.
screens.question: Tap the cells where the walk keeps a letter.

hints.text: Start at the corner, row E, column Y. Do E and Y match?
No match: up and left are both 3, so go up to row G, column Y. Then left to G, G.
Matches on the way: G with G, D with D, E with E.

feedback.correct: G, D, E, read backwards: the subsequence is EDG.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep a letter only where the row letter equals the column letter on the walk.

byKey.r6c2: Row E meets column E there, but the walk never reaches it: it goes up from the corner first.
byKey.r6c5: E and Y differ at the corner, so no letter is kept. Step up.

explain.text: The walk keeps G, then D, then E, so reading forwards gives EDG. Each step moves up, left or both, so it takes at most $m + n$ steps.

screens.title: Write it
screens.prose: Write `lcs_length(a, b)`. The table has one extra row and column for the empty prefixes, so cell `t[i][j]` compares `a[i - 1]` with `b[j - 1]`. It should work for lists as well as strings.
screens.question: Write `lcs_length(a, b)`.

widget.starter:
def lcs_length(a, b):
    m, n = len(a), len(b)
    t = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]
    ...
    return t[m][n]
widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests: empty strings, identical strings, no common letters, two classic pairs, lists of fills, and two 200-letter strings.

hints.text: Loop `i` from 1 to `m` and `j` from 1 to `n`; row 0 and column 0 stay 0.
Compare `a[i - 1]` with `b[j - 1]`: the table is shifted by one.

feedback.correct: One cell per pair of prefixes, each read from three neighbours.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 has an empty string. With the padded table nothing runs and `t[0][3]` is 0.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 has no common letters, so the answer is 0. Add 1 only when the letters match.
byKey.error: If you see `IndexError`, compare `a[i - 1]` with `b[j - 1]`, not `a[i]` with `b[j]`.

explain.text: Each of the $(m + 1)(n + 1)$ cells costs a constant, so the function is $O(mn)$ in time and space. Only `==` is needed between elements, so lists of fills work as well as strings.

screens.title: Off by one
screens.question: What happens on `lcs_length("HEDGE", "EDGY")`?

options.why: You read `a[i]` as the row's letter. Row $i$ is for `a[i - 1]`; `a[i]` is the next letter, and `a[5]` does not exist.

options.text: It returns 2: the shift loses one match
options.why: Before any wrong number comes out, $i = 5$ reads `a[5]`, past the end of HEDGE.
The loop never finishes: `a[5]` does not exist.

hints.text: What is the largest `i` the loop reaches, and how long is HEDGE?
Row $i$ of the table is for the letter `a[i - 1]`.
At `i = 5`, `a[5]` is read. HEDGE has indices 0 to 4.

feedback.correct: At `i = 5` it reads `a[5]`, one past the end.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Trace the largest `i` and `j`.

byKey.three: You expected the right answer. With the padded table, `a[i]` is one letter ahead, and at `i = 5` it runs off the end.
byKey.two: You expected a wrong number. The loop raises an error before returning anything.

explain.text: Row 0 of the table is the empty prefix, so row $i$ holds the letter `a[i - 1]`. Writing `a[i]` compares the wrong letters for $i < 5$ and crashes at $i = 5$. With other loop bounds the same slip gives a silently wrong count, which is worse.

canvas.caption: Row 5 holds a[4], the last E

screens.title: The sibling: edit distance
screens.prose:
You filled $\text{lcs}[i][j] = \text{lcs}[i-1][j-1] + 1$ on a match, else $\max(\text{lcs}[i-1][j], \text{lcs}[i][j-1])$. **Edit distance** counts the fewest inserts, deletes and replaces turning $a$ into $b$, on the same table:

$$d[i][j] = \begin{cases} d[i-1][j-1] & \text{match} \\ 1 + \min(d[i-1][j],\ d[i][j-1],\ d[i-1][j-1]) & \text{else} \end{cases}$$

with $d[i][0] = i$ and $d[0][j] = j$.
screens.question: What is the edit distance from HEDGE to EDGY?

options.why: That is the distance with inserts and deletes only, $5 + 4 - 2 \times 3$. A replace turns the last E into Y in one step.
Deleting H gives EDGE, which still differs from EDGY in its last letter.
You changed every letter outside a matching position. Keep the shared EDG in place.

feedback.correct: Delete H, then replace the final E with Y.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep EDG and count the operations around it.

explain.text: Delete H to get EDGE, then replace E with Y: 2 operations. In the recurrence, up is a delete, left an insert and the diagonal a replace. Diff tools and DNA sequence alignment fill this same table.

screens.title: Write edit distance
screens.prose: Write `edit_distance(a, b)`. The base cases differ from LCS: turning a prefix of length $i$ into the empty string takes $i$ deletes, so the first column counts up, and so does the first row.
screens.question: Write `edit_distance(a, b)`.

widget.starter:
def edit_distance(a, b):
    m, n = len(a), len(b)
    d = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]
    ...
    return d[m][n]
widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests: empty strings on either side, identical strings, ticker spellings from two vendors, and two 150-letter strings.

hints.text: Set `d[i][0] = i` and `d[0][j] = j` before the main loops.
On a match, copy the diagonal with no cost.
Else `d[i][j] = 1 + min(d[i - 1][j], d[i][j - 1], d[i - 1][j - 1])`: delete, insert, replace.

feedback.correct: Same table, a different base and a min instead of a max.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-3: Test 3 turns an empty string into abc: three inserts. Set the first row to `d[0][j] = j`.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 turns abc into an empty string: three deletes. Set the first column to `d[i][0] = i`.
byKey.test-6: Identical strings need 0 edits. On a match, copy the diagonal without adding 1.

explain.text: LCS maximises what is kept and edit distance minimises what changes, on the same $O(mn)$ table. A vendor writing BRK-B for BRK.B is one replace away, which is how fuzzy ticker matching flags likely pairs.

screens.title: Two trade logs that drifted
screens.prose: Our fills and the broker's fills for one stock should agree, in time order. A match must keep that order on both sides. The best order-keeping match is a longest common subsequence.

state.caption: Fills in time order; ids were lost in a vendor change

screens.question: Under the longest in-order match, how many broker fills have no partner in our log?

widget.label: Unmatched broker fills
widget.accept: 2: the LCS has length 5, and the broker log has 7 fills.

hints.text: Find the longest list of fills that appears in order in both logs.
Buy 100, Sell 50, Buy 200, Sell 100, Sell 50 is common to both.
That match has 5 fills. The broker has 7, so $7 - 5$ have no partner.

feedback.correct: Five fills match in order; the broker's extra Buy 100 and Sell 75 do not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the length of the LCS, then subtract it from the broker's count.

byKey.one: You matched by counting fills, 7 against 6. Order matters: Sell 75 has no partner, and one Buy 100 is unmatched.
byKey.lcs: 5 is the length of the match. The question asks for the broker fills left over.

explain.text: `lcs_length(ours, broker)` is 5, so 2 broker fills (a Buy 100 and the Sell 75) need a look, and 1 of ours does too. The same idea compares two versions of a config file line by line.

ideas: $\text{lcs}[i][j]$ is the LCS length of the first $i$ letters of $a$ and the first $j$ of $b$. A padded row and column hold the empty prefixes.
On a match, add 1 to the diagonal; otherwise take the larger of up and left. Walk back from the corner to read the letters.
Edit distance uses the same $O(mn)$ table with $1 + \min$ of delete, insert and replace, and base cases $d[i][0] = i$, $d[0][j] = j$.
summary.trap: With a padded table, row $i$ holds `a[i - 1]`; comparing `a[i]` with `b[j]` is off by one.

options.why: An empty prefix shares nothing: row 0 is all zeros, so this line is right.
No letter matches, so no cell ever adds 1. This line is right.
Identical strings share every letter in order, so this line is right.

feedback.correct: Identical strings have an LCS equal to their length: 3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each line against the table's edges.

explain.text: An empty string or no common letters gives 0. Identical strings match on the whole diagonal, giving their full length.

quiz.prose:
A bug adds 1 to the diagonal even when the letters differ:

```python
t[i][j] = max(t[i - 1][j - 1] + 1, t[i - 1][j], t[i][j - 1])
```
quiz.question: What does it return for `"AB"` and `"CD"`?

options.why: You expected the true answer. The diagonal adds 1 at every cell whether or not the letters match.
The diagonal grows by one per row, and there are only two rows, so it stops at 2.

feedback.correct: It returns 2: the bug counts every diagonal step as a match.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Trace the diagonal: $t[1][1]$, then $t[2][2]$.

explain.text: $t[1][1] = 1$ and $t[2][2] = 2$ although nothing matches. The diagonal adds 1 only on a match.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the fewest single-letter changes.

byKey.two: You replaced and deleted. Deleting the dot alone is enough.

explain.text: Deleting the dot turns `RDS.A` into `RDSA`. A small distance flags the pair for a human to confirm.

quiz.prose: Two config files of 10,000 lines each are compared line by line with the LCS table.
quiz.question: About how many cells does the table have?

options.why: That is the number of lines, $m + n$. The table has a cell for every pair, $m \times n$.
That is the number of subsequences. The table avoids listing them.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the cells: one per pair of prefixes.

explain.text: The table is $O(mn)$. For large files, diff tools use smarter methods that only explore cells near the best path.
